title: The First Screen Rejected 5,206 Candidates. One Run Continued.

voice_performance.performance_intent: A calm lab walkthrough for a beginner; exact results are stated without turning them into a promise.
voice_performance.energy_curve: Immediate recorded result, definitions, measured comparison, explicit limitation, worksheet close.
voice_performance.pause_policy: Brief pauses after counts and thresholds; longer pause before the boundary statement.

sections.label: Start with the screen, not the promise
sections.text: The first screen rejected 5,206 candidates. The same screen started with 5,390 candidate versions. Keep that first total visible. 184 continued. The counts come from three separate runs. The first used Dow futures. The second used S&P 500 futures. The third used EURUSD. Dow supplied all 184 survivors. The other two runs ended at zero. A backtest is a replay of old prices using a stated rule. It asks what would have happened if that rule had been followed across that history. It records one history; tomorrow remains outside this result. A large number can feel like proof. Slow down. This first screen asks a narrow question: did these rules cross the lines on their own historical windows? A pass earns the next question. My read is simple: 184 is a queue, and the next question waits on prices this screen never saw.

sections.label: Follow the actual first screen
sections.text: Now follow one candidate through the path. First, replay the rules. Then measure the result on the development window. The development window is the in-sample window. An in-sample result uses the history that built and screened the rule. This phase replays and measures; it does not optimize a parameter after the fact. Then apply the intake thresholds. A gate is a pass/fail question. A threshold is the line a measurement must cross. A row that passes moves to the next test. It may face later prices. It may face a different fill, a session check, or added costs. Those tests belong later in the pipeline. The records say the data source is real. The wiring proof is true. That means the run reached the part of the pipeline that reads its input. The record says validated=false. The run happened. Live trading is a separate result. Keep the number beside the line it had to cross. That is how the pipeline keeps a result in its place.

sections.label: What counts as a candidate
sections.text: Before the results, make the idea complete. A candidate is one complete set of trading rules. It names the market and timeframe. It says when to enter, how to fill, when to exit, how much to trade, what risk to accept, what costs to pay, and what history to use. Commission is a fee charged for a trade. Slippage is the gap between the reference price and the fill you actually receive. Change one detail and you have a new candidate. Start with an observation. Write the explanations that could account for it. Pick one and write a falsifiable hypothesis. A falsifiable hypothesis is one that could be proved wrong by a defined result. Here, the development window is the in-sample block. Those are the prices used to build and screen the rule. Net profit is what remains after gains, losses, and costs are combined. Gross wins are the winning trade amounts added together before costs. Gross losses are the losing trade amounts added together before costs. Maximum drawdown, or max drawdown, is the largest peak-to-trough fall in the result line. Return-to-drawdown is the recorded return placed beside that largest fall. Profit factor is gross wins divided by gross losses. How often the strategy won is its win rate. Payoff asymmetry means a smaller number of larger wins can outweigh a larger number of smaller losses. Trade count is the number of trades the rule produced. Trades per month is how often the rule acted. A library records these choices; it stores the search choices alongside the measurements. These are measurements of one window. Live performance remains a separate question.

sections.text: Dow is the lane with 184. Of its 1,335 candidates, 1,151 stopped. The failure census counts 1,122 return-to-drawdown failures. It counts 1,065 profit-factor failures. It counts 150 activity failures. The same row can appear in more than one count. Return-to-drawdown is the result compared with the biggest fall from a running high to a later low. This run required a value above 1.0. Profit factor is the comparison of gross winning dollars with gross losing dollars. This run required a value above 1.05. Trades per month is the activity measure in this screen. This run required more than 2 and less than 300 trades per month. Too few trades leave a result hard to measure. Too many can turn costs into the result. Add the three failure counts and you exceed the unique drop because they overlap. A row that misses two lines remains one stopped row. The census records its overlap. The unique number comes from the population: 1,335 entered minus 184 surviving equals 1,151. The visual keeps those ribbons crossing the same population. The thresholds stay attached to this run. A gate can reject a row for any one measured reason. The gate describes this population on this window. It does not set a universal market verdict.

sections.label: One survivor is still only one survivor
sections.text: Here is one row that passed. Its candidate ID is formula-2851293728-1566. Its ledger reports profit factor 1.280370 and return-to-drawdown 4.932417. It has 553 trades. 210 were wins and 343 were losses. How often the strategy won is its win rate, but the winning count alone cannot tell us whether the rule paid for its losing trades. This is payoff asymmetry in a real recorded row: fewer wins can still matter if the winning dollars are larger, while a high win rate can still lose money when losses are larger. Gross wins and gross losses are the dollar piles that profit factor compares. Net profit is the after-cost remainder, and it is one risk measurement among several. sections.label: Search changes the burden of proof
sections.text: Now the selection problem. When you try many versions, chance has more ways to show you an attractive row. The library count tells how many versions were inspected before 184 survived. That denominator belongs beside the survivor, even when the survivor's measurements look clean. Before reading the result, write the hypothesis. Write the complete rule set. Write the data window and costs. Write the measurements and rejection line. Pre-registration is a plan written before reviewing the result, with later changes made visible. That plan is called pre-registration. If a threshold changes after the result appears, give the changed rule a new version. Keep the rejected rows. They show the alternatives tried and the line that stopped them. A survivor carries its search history. Search does not make a row false; it tells us how much selection happened before the row arrived. The first screen answers one narrow question about these versions and windows.

sections.label: 184 is a queue, not a trophy
sections.text: At the boundary, the 184 Dow survivors have one honest description. They are queued for the next test. They passed the previous gate on the development window. Prices after that window have not judged them. The later price block must be fixed before anyone reads its result. That later block is a new test with a separate readout. If rows fail, the first screen still answered its question. If rows continue, live trading remains a separate decision. Survivor means passed the previous gate. Validated=false remains the recorded status. We stop before a later survivor count or payoff. I want to leave you with one question: what happens on prices the pipeline never used to choose these rows?
